prompt: Write 10 distinct lessons the claims-triage agent (home and motor claims assessment within delegated authority) at Larkmere Mutual learned across many cases about: a neighbour's house flooded last winter. Each is a working pattern or tip for the next case, not about any one member, one or two sentences, in the agent's voice ("When…, …"). Return {"items": [{"type": "fact" | "preference" | "observation", "content": "..."}]} with exactly 10 items. (batch 2)
response: {"items":[{"type":"observation","content":"When a neighbour’s property is flooded, I should check early whether the source is likely to be escape of water, surface water or river overflow, because that changes both the likely coverage and the urgency of next steps."},{"type":"fact","content":"When the member reports a winter flood, I should treat freeze-related bursts and delayed seepage as common possibilities and ask about heating, holiday absences and any sign of a pipe or appliance failure."},{"type":"observation","content":"When there is standing water in gardens or on driveways but no obvious internal ingress, I should not assume the home is automatically insured for flood damage; I need to establish whether the damage is to insured property and whether water actually entered the building."},{"type":"preference","content":"When I cannot tell from the first report whether the flood came from the neighbour, a blocked drain or a wider weather event, I prefer to gather a simple timeline first rather than jumping straight to a liability view."},{"type":"observation","content":"When a member says their neighbour was hit hardest, I should remember that adjacency alone does not prove causation, so I need photos, weather context and any signs of local drainage issues before I mark the claim for special handling."},{"type":"fact","content":"When flood water has receded, I should ask whether the member has already taken reasonable drying and salvage steps, because prompt mitigation reduces the chance of avoidable follow-on damage."},{"type":"preference","content":"When the claim includes both flood and escape of water indicators, I prefer to split the questions into source, path and damage, because that keeps the triage clear and avoids missing a second cause."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the neighbour’s home was flooded but the member’s own home only suffered anxiety or inconvenience, I should separate emotional impact from insured loss and only delegate what falls within the policy cover."},{"type":"fact","content":"When winter flooding affects multiple nearby homes, I should expect duplicated reports with similar weather timings, so I need to compare event dates carefully before assuming the same incident applies to every claim."},{"type":"preference","content":"When the case is close to delegated authority limits, I prefer to document the flood source, damage type and any uncertainty in plain language, because a clear file note makes the next decision faster and safer."}]}
